title: Aphids
immediate_actions: Check tender shoots and the undersides of leaves for live aphid colonies.
On sturdy plants, dislodge exposed aphids with a firm spray of plain water.
treatment: Prune small, heavily infested shoots when practical, then inspect new growth again.
Preserve lady beetles, lacewings, and other predators; a small colony on an established plant may need only monitoring.
prevention: Inspect actively growing plants regularly and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer.
Manage ants that protect aphids, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticide use that disrupts natural enemies.

title: Whiteflies
immediate_actions: Inspect leaf undersides for immature whiteflies; flying adults alone do not establish the severity of damage.
Remove a few isolated, heavily infested leaves and check adjacent plants.
treatment: Use a water spray on sturdy plants to reduce exposed adults.
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor activity and preserve predators that help suppress the population.
prevention: Inspect new plants before bringing them into the growing area.
Reduce dust and ant activity, and remove infested annual plants after their productive season.

title: Spider mites
immediate_actions: Inspect leaf undersides with magnification for mites and fine webbing before treating.
Check whether the plant is water-stressed; maintain moisture appropriate for its species.
treatment: Rinse the undersides of infested leaves with plain water where the plant tolerates washing.
Recheck leaves regularly; low populations on woody plants may be controlled by natural predators.
prevention: Reduce dusty conditions around plants and avoid prolonged drought stress.
Protect predatory mites and insects; broad-spectrum insecticides can worsen spider-mite outbreaks.

title: Mealybugs
immediate_actions: Inspect leaf joints, stem crevices, pots, and supports for insects and cottony egg sacs.
Physically remove accessible insects or prune a small infested portion of the plant.
treatment: Use a firm water spray on sturdy plants when insects are exposed, and inspect again over the following days.
If a houseplant remains severely infested, consider discarding it to protect the rest of the collection.
prevention: Inspect new plants, pots, and tools before adding them to the growing area.
Check susceptible plants regularly because hidden colonies can survive an initial removal.

title: Thrips
immediate_actions: Gently tap foliage or flowers over white paper and look for the tiny insects before attributing scars to thrips.
Check fresh growth: old damage can remain after the insects have left.
treatment: On small plants, selectively remove infested shoots rather than shearing all new growth.
Monitor with yellow sticky traps and preserve natural predators; not every thrips species damages plants.
prevention: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer and provide suitable water and light.
Reduce dust and nearby host weeds; seek a plant diagnostic service if a thrips-transmitted virus is suspected.

title: Leaf-feeding caterpillars
immediate_actions: Look for the caterpillar, eggs, droppings, or rolled leaves; chewing damage alone does not identify the pest.
Check how much fresh damage is occurring before taking action.
treatment: Remove identified pest caterpillars and selectively prune rolled or webbed leaves where practical.
Tolerate minor feeding on established plants and preserve natural enemies. Do not treat plants being grown to support butterflies.
prevention: Inspect young growth regularly to find small caterpillars before extensive feeding occurs.
Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that remove beneficial insects and other natural predators.

title: Powdery mildew
immediate_actions: Examine both leaf surfaces for powdery patches and photograph fresh affected growth.
Improve air movement around crowded plants.
treatment: Remove small localized infestations and fallen affected debris where practical.
Provide suitable light and avoid excessive fertilizer; management depends on the host plant and extent of infection.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties when available and space plants for airflow.
Monitor new growth for recurrence. Do not assume powdery mildew and downy mildew need the same management.

title: Rust-like leaf symptoms
immediate_actions: Check lower and inner leaves for raised orange, yellow, or brown powdery spots.
Record which plant species is affected; rust fungi have specific host ranges.
treatment: For garden flowers, remove a limited number of infected leaves without taking more than one-third of the foliage.
Collect affected debris and monitor new growth. Mild rust may be tolerated; existing spots will not disappear with treatment.
prevention: Water the soil instead of the leaves and allow space for air movement.
Use host-appropriate resistant varieties where available; obtain crop-specific advice for fruit trees or field crops.

sources.title: UMN Extension: Rust in the flower garden

title: Leaf spots: general care while confirming the cause
immediate_actions: Photograph both sides of affected leaves and note whether new spots are appearing.
Avoid working among plants while their foliage is wet.
treatment: Remove a few badly affected leaves and fallen debris; do not strip more than one-third of a plant's leaves.
Keep irrigation off foliage and improve spacing. Different fungi, bacteria, and noninfectious injuries can produce similar spots.
prevention: Inspect plants regularly, use healthy planting material, and maintain clean tools.
Use mulch to reduce soil splash and obtain a specific diagnosis if symptoms spread quickly.

sources.title: UMN Extension: Managing plant diseases in the home garden

title: Early blight of tomato or potato
immediate_actions: Confirm that the host is tomato or potato and compare older lower leaves with newer growth.
Keep leaves dry and water at the base of the plant.
treatment: Remove affected leaves selectively, never more than one-third of the plant's foliage.
Clean hands and pruning tools after handling affected plants; use mulch and support plants to reduce soil splash.
prevention: Improve airflow with appropriate spacing, supports, and weed management.
Rotate away from susceptible crops and choose resistant varieties when available. Most home tomatoes tolerate some early blight without fungicide treatment.

sources.title: UMN Extension: Early blight in tomato and potato

title: Root or drainage concerns
immediate_actions: Check soil moisture and drainage before watering again. A leaf photograph cannot confirm root rot or its pathogen.
For a potted plant, check that water can leave the container and that the roots are not sitting in accumulated water.
treatment: Correct drainage and adjust watering to the plant's needs rather than adding water automatically to a wilting plant.
If decline continues, have the roots and growing medium examined before selecting a disease treatment.
prevention: Use an aerated, well-draining growing medium and a container with drainage holes.
Avoid persistently saturated conditions and unnecessarily oversized containers.

title: General monitoring and prevention
immediate_actions: Check the whole plant and both sides of its leaves, rather than relying on one photograph.
Keep a dated photo to compare with new growth.
treatment: When no specific problem is established, continue normal plant care and monitor rather than starting a pesticide treatment.
Seek a plant diagnostic service if symptoms persist, spread, or do not fit the suggested issue.
prevention: Provide species-appropriate light, moisture, spacing, and drainage.
Inspect new plants, clean tools, and check garden plants regularly for early signs of trouble.
